newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire troops block planned student protest route.
newsitem.headline: Zaire troops block planned student protest route.

text.p: Paramilitary security forces in Zaire's capital blocked off main roads leading to campuses where students were due to start a protest march on Tuesday as part of a campaign to oust veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Witnesses said most shops and businesses in the city of five million people remained closed for a second day as Mobutu's opponents stepped up pressure to end his 32-year rule.
After shutting down the capital with a widely observed stay-at-home order on Monday, Mobutu's opponents want to show they, not the cancer-stricken president, are in control.

"It is the opposition, led by Etienne Tshisekedi, that commands. If we ask people to stay at home, they stay at home. If we ask them to go on the streets, they go on the streets," opposition spokesman Laurent Mabyo told Reuters on Monday.

Ousted prime minister Tshisekedi is Mobutu's arch political rival. His followers have resorted to militant street action to end three decades of Mobutu rule while Laurent Kabila's rebels pursue an armed campaign from the east of Zaire.
Kabila's forces have seized nearly half of Africa's third largest country, which is the size of Western Europe, and have declared Kinshasa their immediate target.
The rebels relaunched their drive after a three-day pause to give Mobutu a chance to step down honourably. He brushed aside the ultimatum but left the door open for face-to-face talks with Kabila.
Political analysts say the escalating campaign in Kinshasa is increasingly intended to bolster Tshisekedi's position after what is seen as an inevitable rebel takeover of the capital.
"Tshisekedi played the leading role in ending Mobutu's one- party rule. His followers want to make sure they have a role in a post-Mobutu era," one Zaire watcher told Reuters.
Pro-Tshisekedi protest organisers have asked students to skip school and college and to turn out in vehicles on Tuesday.
In the past, such protests have led to turmoil as students commandeered any vehicles on the street.

Mobutu declared a state of emergency last week, and although Monday's protest sparked no serious incidents, Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba said troops would act to keep order. "Force must be at the service of the law," he told a news briefing after a cabinet meeting devoted to the growing crisis.
Monday's protest closed the capital's shops, schools, and businesses. Public transport was off the streets as were most private vehicles. The business district was deserted.
Security forces were deployed heavily at potential flashpoints. Witnesses said soldiers fired in the air to disperse a crowd near Tshisekedi's home but there were no reports of major violence.
As the protest crippled the capital on Monday, Kabila entered Zaire's second city Lubumbashi in triumph to celebrate the fall of the copper capital to his forces last week.

With the fall of Lubumbashi, Kinshasa is the only major city still under the control of Mobutu's ragged army, which has collapsed in the face of the rebellion launched on Zaire's eastern border in October.
